This surprising brain difference may explain why some kids struggle with math: Study Stanford researchers have found that children who consistently struggle with mathematics may have underlying differences in the way their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia took longer to switch between strategies, were less responsive to changes in difficulty and found it harder to improve their approaches over time, as per the ScienceDaily website. ANI | Updated: 13-11-2026 23:15 IST | Created: 13-11-2026 23:15 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Stanford researchers have found that children who consistently struggle with mathematics may have underlying differences in the way their brains manage problem-solving strategies. Children with developmental dyscalculia took longer to switch between strategies, were less responsive to changes in difficulty and found it harder to improve their approaches over time, as per the ScienceDaily website. Researchers also identified distinct patterns of brain activity associated with these challenges, which could predict certain math-related abilities. For some children, learning math is much more difficult than it is for their classmates. Even when they practice and receive instruction, they may continue to struggle with problems that other children their age can solve more easily. Researchers are now uncovering clues about why these difficulties persist, and the answers may involve more than an understanding of numbers. One possible explanation lies in differences in how the brain selects and manages strategies for solving problems. A new study from Stanford University suggests that children with persistent math difficulties may have trouble adjusting their approach when faced with different mathematical challenges. The researchers also identified distinctive patterns of brain activity associated with these struggles, as per ScienceDaily website. The findings, published in JNeurosci, come from research led by Oliver Lasnick and colleagues at Stanford University. Their work focused on children with a condition that causes ongoing difficulty with mathematical problem solving (developmental dyscalculia). Although the condition has been recognized for years, scientists are still working to understand the specific thinking processes and brain mechanisms that contribute to it. Why Some Children Struggle With Math Strategies To investigate these challenges, the Stanford team studied 68 children between the ages of 8 and 10. They examined how the children approached math problems, how effectively they used different strategies, and how their brain activity related to their performance. Solving a math problem often requires more than knowing numbers or remembering arithmetic facts. Children must also decide which approach will work best. For example, a child might count individual numbers to find an answer or use a more efficient method based on a familiar mathematical relationship. As problems become more difficult, the ability to recognize when a different strategy is needed can become increasingly important. The researchers found that children with developmental dyscalculia were generally less effective at using different mathematical strategies than children without the condition. They took longer to shift from one method to another and were less responsive when the difficulty of a problem changed. According to ScienceDaily website, another important difference involved learning to choose better strategies over time. While other children became more effective at selecting appropriate approaches, those with developmental dyscalculia did not show the same improvement. This suggests that their difficulties may involve not only performing calculations but also deciding how to approach a problem in the first place. Brain Activity Reveals New Clues to Math Difficulties The researchers also examined patterns of brain activity to better understand what might be happening behind these behavioral differences. They discovered that activity within a particular brain system differed between children with developmental dyscalculia and those who were more skilled at selecting and using math strategies. These neural patterns were not simply unrelated differences. They could also predict how effectively children counted and how well they switched between approaches when solving problems. The findings highlight the possible importance of several mental abilities that extend beyond mathematics itself. These include attention, memory, and cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to adjust thinking or behavior when circumstances change. Such abilities are part of what researchers often call executive functions. These mental processes help people organize information, stay focused on a task, hold relevant details in mind, and change plans when an approach is not working. In mathematics, they can help a child keep track of numbers, compare possible solutions, and recognize when to try a different method, as per the study published on the website. The Stanford findings suggest that difficulties involving these processes may contribute to the development of dyscalculia. Differences in brain activity may also help explain why some children have persistent trouble choosing and changing problem-solving strategies. However, the observed connections do not establish that the brain activity differences directly cause the condition. They provide new evidence about the cognitive and neural processes associated with these mathematical difficulties. Understanding Why Math Struggles Differ Between Children An important conclusion is that developmental dyscalculia does not appear to involve one simple problem shared by every affected child. Instead, different children may experience difficulties involving several interacting mental processes. As Lasnick explains, "Importantly, this study also emphasizes the individual variability observed in dyscalculia, further demonstrating that the disorder reflects cognitive and neural dysfunction across multiple processes." By connecting children's mathematical behavior with measurable differences in brain activity, the research offers a more detailed picture of why math can be persistently challenging for some students. The findings also point toward the importance of looking beyond whether a child gets the correct answer. Understanding how children choose strategies, adapt to more difficult problems, and manage the mental demands of mathematics could ultimately help researchers develop better ways to identify and support those with developmental dyscalculia, as per the study published on the ScienceDaily website. (ANI)

item.content:encoded:
Taiwan accuses China of pressuring Papua New Guinea to expel Taiwanese diplomats During a legislative hearing on Thursday, Lin Hung-hsun, Deputy Director-General of Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs Department of East Asian and Pacific Affairs, said PNG initially demanded the closure of Taiwan's representative office on July 16, citing its adherence to the "one-China" policy. ANI | Updated: 13-11-2026 21:53 IST | Created: 13-11-2026 21:53 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Taiwan has accused China of pressuring Papua New Guinea (PNG) to expel Taiwanese diplomats and shut down its representative office in Port Moresby, alleging that Beijing may have used economic incentives to influence the Pacific nation's sudden diplomatic decision, according to a report by Central News Agency (CNA). During a legislative hearing on Thursday, Lin Hung-hsun, Deputy Director-General of Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs Department of East Asian and Pacific Affairs, said PNG initially demanded the closure of Taiwan's representative office on July 16, citing its adherence to the "one-China" policy. According to CNA, Taiwan and PNG subsequently held discussions and reached an understanding that PNG would provide one year's written notice before the representative office was closed. However, on November 6, PNG reportedly reversed its earlier position and demanded that Taiwanese diplomats leave the country within seven days. Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi told lawmakers that Taiwan believed the sudden change in PNG's position was driven by pressure from Beijing. He pointed to a recent visit by a high-level PNG delegation to China and the upcoming visit of PNG Prime Minister James Marape to China to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit. "Given these circumstances, our assessment is that the government of Papua New Guinea may have been subjected to significant pressure from China or even offered economic incentives," Chen said, as cited by CNA. Chen also highlighted China's announcement that it was prepared to increase imports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from PNG. This came after Taiwan decided to stop purchasing LNG from the Pacific nation following its demand to close the Taiwanese representative office. The diplomatic dispute concerns the Taiwan Economic Office, which was established in Port Moresby in 1990. On November 6, PNG's Department of Foreign Affairs announced that its secretary, Elias Wohengu, had instructed the office's head, Chiu Chen-yu, and First Secretary Lee Chung-nun to leave the country within seven days. The remaining diplomat, Pan Shao-jyun, was permitted to stay to oversee the office's closure within a year. PNG's foreign affairs department also clarified that although Taiwan had been given 12 months to complete the closure, this should not be interpreted as a guarantee that existing staffing and operational arrangements would remain unchanged during that period. In response, Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) announced that it would shut down the representative office and withdraw all personnel stationed in PNG. The ministry also said it would conduct a comprehensive review and adjustment of its relations with PNG, taking into account Taiwan's national dignity, diplomatic autonomy and overall national interests. According to CNA, Taiwan has since begun withdrawing its diplomatic and technical mission personnel from the Pacific nation. PNG maintains diplomatic relations with China, which follows a policy of not allowing its diplomatic allies to maintain simultaneous official diplomatic relations with Taiwan. The latest developments have further highlighted Beijing's diplomatic pressure on countries maintaining or considering engagement with Taipei. (ANI)

item.content:encoded:
US Treasury chief says Fed should not hike rates over energy shock tied to Iran war Reuters | Updated: 13-11-2026 19:25 IST | Created: 13-11-2026 19:25 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that the Federal Reserve should have an open mind and not hike rates because of an "energy supply shock" tied to the Iran war. "I think the Fed should understand that this is an energy supply shock," while the underlying US economy is very strong, Bessent said in an interview on CNBC. "So I think that to hike too much into an energy supply shock when it's coming down, these are very noisy numbers," he said. "You know, the Fed's supposed to look into the future, not look in the rearview mirror." A stronger-than-expected US jobs report last week bolstered the case for further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, which had lost some momentum amid a post-election stock market selloff and growing fears that weaker AI-driven demand could undercut the economy. The US central bank left its policy rate on hold last month, with Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh saying policymakers would be watching for data to help decide whether more monetary policy tightening would be needed. "I'm not going to tell the Fed what to do. I am going to say they should have an open mind," Bessent said. The Fed did three rate cuts over the same period last year, he noted. "And now to reverse just based on an energy supply shock, a reversal in a dramatic way isn't something that I would do if I were on the Fed. But I'm not on the Fed."

item.content:encoded:
Global oil market to return to surplus in Q4 2026, larger supply build expected in 2027: IEA The global oil market is expected to return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of 2026, with a larger surplus anticipated in 2027 as production recovers faster than demand, according to the International Energy Agency's (IEA) November Oil Market Report. ANI | Updated: 13-11-2026 16:57 IST | Created: 13-11-2026 16:57 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The global oil market is expected to return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of 2026, with a larger surplus anticipated in 2027 as production recovers faster than demand, according to the International Energy Agency's (IEA) November Oil Market Report. The report highlighted that global oil supplies have surpassed demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran, signalling a gradual rebalancing of international oil markets. "Our November supply and demand balances suggest that the global oil market will return to a surplus in 4Q26, with a more substantial build in 2027," the IEA stated. According to the report, global oil demand is projected to decline by 2.7 million barrels per day (mb/d) in 2026 to 102.3 mb/d before rebounding by 2 mb/d in 2027. The agency noted that the pace of demand contraction is expected to moderate to 2.7 mb/d year-on-year in the fourth quarter of 2026, compared with declines of 5 mb/d in the second quarter and 3.8 mb/d in the third quarter. Global oil demand is expected to return to growth around March 2027 as supply chains normalise and disruptions to petroleum product exports from the Gulf gradually ease. The report stated that liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), ethane and naphtha would account for nearly 80 per cent of the projected demand increase in 2027, while transport fuels would register modest growth. On the supply side, global oil production increased by 2.3 mb/d in October to 105.4 mb/d, following a rise of 3 mb/d in September, supported by recovering oil exports from the Gulf. Gulf oil exports, excluding Oman, reached 18.4 mb/d in October, although they remained 26 per cent below pre-war levels. Crude oil shipments increased to 15 mb/d, equivalent to 82 per cent of pre-war levels. The recovery prompted the IEA to revise its global oil supply estimates for the fourth quarter of 2026 upward by 3.3 mb/d. For the full year, global oil supply is expected to decline by 4.8 mb/d in 2026 before recovering sharply by 6.6 mb/d to an average of 108.1 mb/d in 2027. Meanwhile, international crude oil prices have witnessed a sharp correction as recovering Gulf exports eased supply constraints. The report noted that North Sea Dated crude oil prices declined by approximately 32 per cent from a peak of USD 136 per barrel in early October to around USD 93 per barrel at the time of writing. However, crude prices remained approximately USD 22 per barrel above their pre-war levels. Despite easing crude prices, the IEA warned that tight supplies of refined petroleum products, particularly diesel, continue to pose challenges for global energy markets. European diesel prices declined by 11 per cent over the same period but remained close to USD 180 per barrel, approximately 77 per cent above pre-war levels. Global refinery activity weakened in October, with refinery runs declining by 1.3 mb/d month-on-month to 81.3 mb/d. However, refinery throughput is expected to recover to 84.7 mb/d by December 2026. The IEA also highlighted a recovery in global oil inventories, with observed stocks increasing by 52 million barrels in October, marking their first monthly rise since June. However, on-land inventories continued to decline and remained at their lowest levels since at least 2016. Looking ahead, the IEA cautioned that continued attacks on shipping could threaten the recovery in global oil supplies and undermine maritime security. The agency added that the accelerated release of IEA emergency diesel stocks over the coming months would help bridge supply gaps until global refinery operations and petroleum product output recover. (ANI)
